analysis.one_liner: Gives Medicare patients earlier access to FDA-designated breakthrough medical devices through four years of temporary coverage.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee advanced the bill 37–3 in September 2025, three days after it was introduced; neither chamber has voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new Medicare pathway for devices the FDA has designated as "breakthrough" — devices meant to treat or diagnose life-threatening or seriously debilitating conditions. Once CMS designates such a device, Medicare would cover it for four years without waiting for the agency's usual, often lengthy, national coverage decision. CMS would have six months to rule on each manufacturer's application and must make a final permanent coverage decision before the four-year window ends for manufacturers who ask in time.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with life-threatening or seriously debilitating conditions gain faster access to newly approved devices, without waiting the months or years it can take CMS to issue its own coverage decision. Medical device manufacturers gain a guaranteed four-year Medicare payment stream for designated devices, and providers gain new billable services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients awaiting new medical devices

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover FDA-designated breakthrough devices for four years starting when CMS designates them, so seniors with life-threatening or debilitating conditions could get new devices without waiting for a national coverage decision.
CMS must decide designation applications within six months, and if it says no it must give the manufacturer a written explanation of exactly which criteria the device failed.

Manufacturers who request a national coverage determination early enough are guaranteed a final decision before the four-year transition ends, so temporary coverage cannot quietly become permanent without a ruling.

The bill includes guardrails: devices must otherwise qualify for Medicare coverage, must not present an undue risk of harm that outweighs benefits for seniors, and devices cleared through the 510(k) pathway must have been cleared using clinical data that included Medicare beneficiaries. CMS can also review providers with aberrant billing patterns for these devices.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare (and ultimately taxpayers and beneficiaries through premiums and cost-sharing) would pay for the devices themselves during the four-year transition, plus $10 million a year through FY2030 for CMS to run the new program. Beneficiaries also pay their usual Medicare coinsurance on devices whose benefit is not yet fully established.

drawbacks.text: Medicare would pay for these devices for up to four years before CMS makes its own evidence-based national coverage determination — during the transition, coverage turns on the designation criteria rather than a finding that the device works better than existing treatments.

The designation criteria do not require proof that the device outperforms the care seniors already receive, only that it would otherwise be covered and does not present undue risk, so Medicare and its beneficiaries could spend heavily on devices whose advantage is unproven.

The bill appropriates $10 million a year through FY2030 for implementation, on top of whatever Medicare pays for the devices themselves, and beneficiaries pay their usual coinsurance on devices whose benefit is not yet fully established.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare patients with serious conditions and few options, faster access to newly approved devices is a real gain, and the bill builds in safeguards plus a hard deadline for a permanent coverage decision. The trade-off is money and risk: Medicare pays for up to four years before its own evidence review decides whether the device actually works better, and beneficiaries share the cost of devices whose advantage over existing care is unproven. Whether the access gain justifies that depends heavily on how strictly CMS applies the risk and clinical-data criteria — and the bill does not require proof of superiority over existing treatments.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Ways and Means Committee 37-3 on September 17, 2025 and now waits for action by the full House, with the Energy and Commerce Committee still holding its own referral.

narrative.text: Rep. Blake Moore introduced the bill on September 15, 2025 with five bipartisan original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to two committees — Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce — which means two committees must act before it can reach the floor.
On September 17, 2025, the Ways and Means Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 37-3.
As of the latest action, the bill has not received a vote in the full House or Senate, and the Energy and Commerce Committee has not acted on its portion.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the bill's bipartisan sponsors and the medical device industry: the bill cleared its first committee 37-3 within days of introduction with no opposition on the record. If it becomes law, Medicare patients with serious conditions and device makers would both gain, though Medicare would bear the cost of paying for devices before its own evidence review is complete.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bipartisan sponsors and medical device makers, so far

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee

sides.party_line_note: Support split almost evenly across parties: 33 of 223 Republicans and 32 of 217 Democrats cosponsored, and the committee approved it 37-3.

industries.note: The bill gives device makers a statutory guarantee of Medicare payment for four years for designated devices, without the usual national coverage determination first — and creates a permanent designation pathway with deadlines CMS must meet. Patients gain faster access, but the industry gains revenue before Medicare's own evidence review confirms the device works better than existing care.

industries.industry: Hospitals and providers that furnish the devices
industries.note: Hospitals and physician practices could bill Medicare for newly designated devices during the transition period. This expands their billable services, though the bill lets CMS scrutinize providers with aberrant billing patterns for these devices.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is off to an unusually fast start — a committee report three days after introduction and 65 bipartisan cosponsors. Bills like this often reach the House floor, sometimes attached to larger health legislation, but the outstanding Energy and Commerce referral and the Senate's inaction on similar Medicare-coverage bills in recent Congresses mean final passage is far from certain.
